title: A Responsible Innovation Approach to Technology Assessment. The Case of Artificial Intelligence: Natural Language Processing Methods for Identifying Impacts and Risks of Emerging Technologies
abstract: This thesis addresses the pressing issue of sustainable implementation and functioning of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within society, focusing on the broader, indirect, or unintended side effects of AI technologies.AI continues to evolve rapidly and becomes more deeply embedded in various sectors.Consequently, there is an urgent need to understand not only the immediate benefits but also the extensive societal impacts that extend beyond the direct, functional applications of AI.Although much contemporary research has focused on optimizing AI for the social good, a significant gap remains in measuring and addressing the wider-reaching consequences of these technologies.This gap is particularly evident in understanding their environmental, social, and economic side effects.The primary research questions that guide this study are the following: What are the effects that AI systems produce on society and how can we evaluate the positive and negative effects of AI adoption?This research employs a comprehensive set of datasets, including Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) reports, AI patents, firm-level financial data, documented AI incidents, foundation models' release reports, and AI policy documents.Through a combination of machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), regression models, and average treatment effect (ATE) calculations, alongside qualitative analyses of risk mitigation strategies, the study examines the social, environmental, and economic consequences of AI technologies, as well as actual and potential harms.The empirical results demonstrate that firms adopting AI technologies generate substantially greater sustainability impacts compared to non-AI firms, in economic, environmental, and social dimensions.The study reveals that existing risk mitigation techniques tend to focus predominantly on direct observable risks, leaving significant side effects underexamined in scientific, development, and policy discourse.This underscores a critical blind spot in current AI governance.The thesis aims to contribute a new method for evaluating the sustainability impacts produced by firms utilizing AI technologies, and a taxonomy for identifying and categorizing AI-related risks based on system function and user intention.These contributions advance the literature on Responsible Innovation, emphasizing the need to integrate indirect AI effects into broader governance frameworks.The thesis also conv ceptualizes AI as a form of simulation, arguing that well-functioning General Purpose AI Systems (GPAIS) may pose existential risks that are inadequately addressed by current mitigation techniques.The findings highlight the urgency of expanding our understanding of the indirect effects of AI and provide actionable managerial and policy recommendations aimed at fostering positive impacts on sustainability while mitigating associated risks.These recommendations call for the development of more comprehensive AI governance frameworks that account for long-term effects throughout the entire social system.Future research is suggested to further investigate the mechanisms by which AI impacts emerge and to develop more robust tools to assess these effects in a broader social context.This will ensure the sustainable integration of AI technologies into society, balancing innovation with responsibility.
